moves.spoken: White opens with the Nimzowitsch-Larsen, b3. The classical reply is to occupy the centre at once — e5.
He develops, and the knight to f3 attacks our pawn on e5.
Rather than defend it, we push the pawn forward to e4.
This is a well-known, fully legitimate theoretical line — and a very complex one. White's hypermodern idea is to tempt our pawns forward now so he can attack them later.
We don't capture the knight — instead the queen comes to f6 to chase it. It may look like we're pinning ourselves...
...but because his bishop was hanging, the knight was forced to run specifically to c4.
And we reposition the queen to g6.
He's blitzing his moves out, shuffling the same knight again and again in the opening.
There's no reason to be intimidated by an opponent who flouts opening principles — you simply obey them yourself. The knight comes to f6.
He plays g3. The way to punish this kind of play is precisely to follow opening principles to the letter.
What have we not done yet? Completed development, and fully occupied the centre with pawns. So d5, building a big central pawn chain.
He fianchettoes with the bishop to g2. Now all that remains is to bring our pieces out.
We develop the bishop to e6 first, reinforcing the centre.
He castles. This is the instructive moment: we could keep developing or castle long — but notice White has completely neglected his queenside development.
Even though we're not fully developed either, we're ready to start attacking — so h5, aiming to pry open the h-file.
He answers with h4, but that only softens his kingside further.
Now we castle long, completing our development — and mark that pawn on g3; sacrifices are in the air.
He lunges with a4 — very creative, but not objectively sound.
The refutation is patience: don't panic, finish developing, and only attack once you're ready. The bishop swings to d6.
He plays the king to h2, walking right into it. We're eyeing a knight check on g4 — though he can capture the knight.
But that's the point: the knight checks on g4, and after he takes, we recapture with the pawn, ripping open the h-file — exactly what we wanted.
Now we threaten to grab his pawn, and he's forced to drop the king back toward g1.
That retreat was his only serious move; instead he lets us capture on h4 with check.
But don't rush the capture — first the bishop steps to e5, out of the sticky spot it was in.
Now we take on h4 with check, and head for a beautiful little finale.
This is what happens when you shamelessly violate opening principles. After the king to g1, there's a lovely way to finish.
The queen swings to h6...
...sacrificing the rook.
Despite being a whole rook down, Black's pressure on the kingside is absolutely overwhelming.
We're threatening mate; his only way to stave it off is the rook to e1.
But after g3, all of our pieces come pouring in.
If he tries e3, we can simply take the rook, winning the material back...
...or play the bishop to g4. The position is overflowing with mating ideas — completely crushing, which is why he resigned.
A note on the opening: the Nimzowitsch-Larsen itself is not a bad opening at all. Pushing the knight to e5 was the inaccuracy...
...the knight to d4 is the better move, because from there it can be supported with e3.

The real lesson: strong players can bend opening principles strategically and still get a decent position — that's what modern chess is about — but it's very hard without experience. Get comfortable with sensible, classical openings first; only then start experimenting.

Here d4 would have been interesting, at least staking a claim in the centre. Instead he drifted — the knight to c4, then to e3, ignoring development when e3 or d3 was called for. Then h5 softened him up, and that pawn cost him the game; opening the h-file was a disaster. d3 was his last fighting chance — but after the king to h2, it walked straight into the pin.
